name: Rotate to Carni
description: Rotating to Carni seeks a leg-assisted shoulder clamp after clearing the high leg around the head and turning partly belly down with triceps and wrist control.
summary: Rotating to Carni seeks a leg-assisted shoulder clamp after clearing the high leg around the head and turning partly belly down with triceps and wrist control.
overview:
The bottom guard player begins in New York with a safe neck-clearing angle, facing a top player whose posture is controlled. Richie Martinez demonstrates the shoulder-lock mechanics through Jersey from Z guard. A direct New York entry is a positional adaptation, not established by that lesson alone.

Use the guard and shoulder connection to bring the opponent close before moving the high leg. Manage the shoulder and neck line with a forearm frame as the leg clears the head. Turn partly belly down with the knee close and foot supported rather than wrenching the leg across the head.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Richie Martinez — Carni shoulder lock from Z guard](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iClQ2Np-n30).

attacker.description: Rotate to Carni (attacker): Use the guard and shoulder connection to bring the opponent close before moving the high leg. Manage the shoulder and neck line with a forearm frame as the leg clears the head.
attacker.overview:
The bottom guard player begins in New York with a safe neck-clearing angle, facing a top player whose posture is controlled. Richie Martinez demonstrates the shoulder-lock mechanics through Jersey from Z guard. A direct New York entry is a positional adaptation, not established by that lesson alone.

Use the guard and shoulder connection to bring the opponent close before moving the high leg. Manage the shoulder and neck line with a forearm frame as the leg clears the head. Turn partly belly down with the knee close and foot supported rather than wrenching the leg across the head.

Keep the captured arm connected so the opponent cannot freely roll or withdraw the shoulder. Hold the wrist and elbow at a comfortable angle; a small change can load the shoulder rapidly. Release the wrist and leg clamp immediately on a tap or when the partner needs to roll safely.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Hip movement turns the supported knee and torso into the shoulder clamp while the neck frame blocks forward chest pressure. Carni is a rotational lock and a new submission entry: the triceps connection must prevent the arm withdrawing before any finishing angle is considered.

Hold the triceps: Keep the captured arm connected so the opponent cannot freely roll or withdraw the shoulder.
Control before finishing: Hold the wrist and elbow at a comfortable angle; a small change can load the shoulder rapidly.
Let the lock go: Release the wrist and leg clamp immediately on a tap or when the partner needs to roll safely.

defender.name: Rotate to Carni Defender
defender.description: Rotate to Carni (defender): A leg clearing the head with an overhook is an upper-body trap, even if a butterfly hook remains below. Avoid reaching away while the opponent sets the triceps control.
defender.overview:
The bottom guard player begins in New York with a safe neck-clearing angle, facing a top player whose posture is controlled. Richie Martinez demonstrates the shoulder-lock mechanics through Jersey from Z guard. A direct New York entry is a positional adaptation, not established by that lesson alone.

A leg clearing the head with an overhook is an upper-body trap, even if a butterfly hook remains below. Avoid reaching away while the opponent sets the triceps control. Maintain a balanced base and a safe inside frame before the shoulder becomes clamped.

Create slack around the shoulder and elbow before moving the hips past the legs. Do not force a forward roll when the triceps and wrist are fixed; tap if pressure has already engaged. Raise the head and chest only after the arm and head-side leg are clear.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

An early escape removes the triceps and leg connections before the shoulder is fixed. Keep the arm aligned until it is free; standing or rolling against the clamp adds rotation instead of releasing it.
key_principles: Identify the shoulder threat: A leg clearing the head with an overhook is an upper-body trap, even if a butterfly hook remains below.
Keep the elbow close early: Avoid reaching away while the opponent sets the triceps control.
Deny the belly-down angle: Maintain a balanced base and a safe inside frame before the shoulder becomes clamped.
Free the arm before passing: Create slack around the shoulder and elbow before moving the hips past the legs.
Avoid rolling against the lock: Do not force a forward roll when the triceps and wrist are fixed; tap if pressure has already engaged.
Rebuild posture after release: Raise the head and chest only after the arm and head-side leg are clear.
